newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Canadian envoy told HK will stay "distinctive".
newsitem.headline: Canadian envoy told HK will stay "distinctive".

text.p: Canada's foreign minister ended a visit to China and Hong Kong on Saturday saying he had been promised that Hong Kong's distinctive character would be preserved after it reverts to China in July.

"One thing I thought to me was very encouraging was the notion that there would be in the future a real distinctive Hong Kong way of doing things...and that the decisions about Hong Kong will be made by Hong Kong itself," said Lloyd Axworthy.

He met Hong Kong Governor Chris Patten and future leader Tung Chee-hwa on Saturday, after meeting Chinese Premier Li Peng, Foreign Minister Qian Qichen and the top Chinese official for Hong Kong Lu Ping in Beijing earlier this week.

"There was very strong determination that whatever the decisions will be, and no one can forecast those, that they will be very much in the interest of retaining the autonomous position, living up to the two systems theory in one country," Axworthy told a news conference before returning to Canada.
Britain returns Hong Kong to China on July 1, ending more than 150 years of colonial rule.

The Basic Law, a Beijing-imposed constitution for post-handover Hong Kong, guarantees that the territory can function as a separate entity from the rest of China for 50 years after the transfer of sovereignty.

Axworthy said China had told him during his visit that commitments to the Basic Law and International Covenants on rights would be adhered to in Hong Kong. "We were given again assurances that those commitments will be fulfilled."

He raised the issue of civil liberties with Tung, who backs China's plan to curb certain Hong Kong civil rights. The plan has drawn loud opposition, especially from the territory's Democratic Party, which has urged Canada to stand up for civil rights.
"We got assurances that there would be a consultation process on it (the plan) as well," Axworthy said.

The Canadian minister was also told Hong Kong will hold elections before July 1 next year for a new legislature to succeed a China-appointed provisional body which will replace, upon the handover, the present elected Legislative Council.
Axworthy welcomed China's decision to give Hong Kong emigrants a grace period to return to the territory if they want to keep permanent residency rights.

He said he got the impression from both Beijing and Tung that the grace period would be sufficiently long, and China would specify the length "fairly shortly". About 350,000 Hong Kong people have emigrated to Canada since 1970.
Axworthy said Beijing had assured him visa-free access for Canadians visiting Hong Kong after July 1, after Canada granted visa-free entry to holders of Hong Kong's post-handover passports.
